subject: design
source_evidence: Grounded in the skill body (Coverage — fidelity ladder, fidelity matching, learning-goal contract, sacrificial concepts; Philosophy; Verification; Do NOT Use When).

cases.scenario: A team wants to learn whether a new onboarding flow is understandable. A designer has scoped a two-week, fully styled, clickable high-fidelity build in Figma to test it.
cases.context: The underlying assumption being tested is roughly a one-week bet; visuals are not the question.
cases.question: How should the agent advise on fidelity and approach?
expected_flags: Match fidelity to the question — flow understandability is answerable at low fidelity (paper sketch / rough wireframe)
Flag the two-week high-fi build as over-fidelity: construction time should be small relative to the cost of being wrong
Note high fidelity prematurely anchors stakeholders on visuals and risks the prototype becoming the product
Write the learning question and success evidence first
expected_fix_hints: Drop to paper/wireframe to test comprehension of the flow
Reserve clickable/high-fi for questions only it can answer (e.g. find-the-primary-action)
absent_signals: Do not default to the highest fidelity available
Do not skip writing the learning question

cases.scenario: Before building any recommendation engine, the team wants to know whether users will trust and act on an AI-suggested product category.
cases.context: Building the real engine is weeks of work; the open question is human trust, not algorithmic accuracy.
cases.question: What prototype should the agent propose?
expected_flags: Propose a wizard-of-oz prototype — a human secretly performs the suggestion the system will later automate
Lets the team measure trust/behavior before the engine exists
Start from the written learning question (will users trust/act on the suggestion?) and the evidence that answers it
Avoid building the engine just to test the trust question
expected_fix_hints: Stage a session where a person feeds 'AI' suggestions behind the interface
Define in advance what reaction counts as 'trusted' vs 'not'
absent_signals: Do not build the production recommendation engine to test trust
Do not run the test without a defined evidence bar

cases.scenario: A team books a usability session for next week and is building a clickable prototype, but when asked what they want to learn the answer is 'we just want feedback, make it look good.'
cases.context: No written question or success/failure definition exists yet.
cases.question: How should the agent proceed before construction continues?
expected_flags: Stop and write the learning-goal contract first: one or two questions the prototype must answer
Define what evidence would count as an answer in either direction before building
Without it, the test produces ambiguous results ('let's just make it look nice')
Then pick the lowest fidelity that answers the agreed question
expected_fix_hints: Draft the one or two learning questions and the evidence bar
Choose fidelity from the question, not from the calendar
absent_signals: Do not proceed to build without a written question
Do not equate 'make it look good' with a learning goal

cases.scenario: A 'high-fidelity prototype' tested well, and leadership now wants to harden that exact Figma-exported code and ship it to production to save time.
cases.context: The prototype was built to answer a concept question, not to be the production artifact.
cases.question: How should the agent respond?
expected_flags: A prototype that ships becomes a product — that is engineering implementation, not prototyping
Prototypes are disposable by design; there should be no implicit commitment that it becomes production
Hardening throwaway prototype code into production carries quality-bar, lifecycle, and maintenance debt
Treat the prototype's learning as the output and build the production version with proper engineering
expected_fix_hints: Carry forward the validated decisions, not the prototype artifact
Build the ship-ready feature through engineering implementation / design-module-composition where reuse applies
absent_signals: Do not ship the throwaway prototype as the product
Do not treat passing a concept test as production-readiness

cases.scenario: A teammate asks the prototyping skill to build a polished, reusable dashboard-widget component to add to the design system library so other teams can drop it in.
cases.context: The request is framed as 'prototype the widget' but the intent is a durable shared component.
cases.question: How should the agent scope this request?
expected_flags: Reusable, ship-and-reuse components are out of scope — that is design-module-composition
Prototyping produces disposable artifacts for learning, with a different lifecycle, quality bar, and audience
Redirect to design-module-composition rather than building a production-grade shared component
If there is an open learning question, a throwaway prototype could test it first — but the durable component itself is not prototyping
expected_fix_hints: Hand the durable component work to design-module-composition
Only prototype if there is an unanswered question worth a disposable test
absent_signals: Do not build the production design-system component under the prototyping skill
Do not treat 'add to the library' as a learning goal

cases.scenario: The team has a live feature in production and wants to find out where users get stuck in the checkout flow.
cases.context: The artifact already exists and is shipped; no new concept is being explored.
cases.question: How should the agent handle this?
expected_flags: No new prototype is required — there is already a real artifact to evaluate
Use usability-testing directly on the existing feature
Prototyping is for building a thing to answer a question, not for testing finished work
Redirect to usability-testing rather than rebuilding the flow as a prototype
expected_fix_hints: Run usability-testing on the production checkout flow
Reserve prototyping for an unbuilt concept or a redesign hypothesis
absent_signals: Do not build a prototype of an already-shipped flow just to test it
Do not conflate usability-testing with prototyping
